title: Your Listing vs. the Model Home: A Texas Staging Game Plan for 2026
summary: Stage your Texas listing to compete with new builds: 2026 market numbers, the rooms Texas buyers want to see, Texas-ready bundles and MLS photo tips.
body_markdown:
Scouting report


## Buyers aren't in a hurry anymore


Remember when Texas homes had offers before the sign was even in the yard? Those days have cooled off. In August, the average Texas home took **65 days** to sell, and there were enough homes for sale to last more than five months.


With that many choices, buyers get picky. They scroll past empty rooms and save the ones that already feel like home. (Not just a hunch: in NAR's 2025 staging report, 83% of buyers' agents said staging helps buyers picture the home as their own.)


Sources: Texas Real Estate Research Center,[Texas Housing Insight, October 2026](https://trerc.tamu.edu/reports/texas-housing-insight-october-2026/) ; NAR[2025 Profile of Home Staging](https://www.nar.realtor/sites/default/files/2025-05/2025-profile-of-home-staging-05-06-2025.pdf) ; Texas REALTORS[Texas Relocation Report](https://www.texasrealestate.com/about-us/newsroom/news-releases/texas-had-the-second-highest-share-of-state-to-state-moves/) .


1st quarter


## The living room: make the first photo count


Buyers decide in a few seconds whether to keep clicking, and the first photo is usually the living room. Empty, it's just bare floors and a fireplace nobody's sitting by. The **Brookside** bundle adds a cream sofa, two leather armchairs the color of a well-worn saddle, and a soft rug. It feels like a weekend in the Hill Country, minus the traffic on 290.


Before


After


Other good fits under Living Room: **Hideout** , **Navarro** , and **Hilltop** .


2nd quarter


## The game room: give it a purpose


In Texas, the upstairs game room is practically a requirement. But empty, buyers can't tell if it's an office, a gym, or the place where the kids' toys go to multiply. The **Wheatfield** bundle (under Media Room) makes it the spot for game day, with leather recliners (cup holders included, naturally), a wood TV wall, and a big cozy rug. Cowboys or Texans? We're staying out of that one.


Before


After


That's halftime, and your listing is already tied with the model home.


Halftime


## What's allowed in Texas


Good news: as of November 2026, Texas has no special law about virtually staged photos. The Texas Real Estate Commission's rule is simple: your ads can't give buyers the wrong idea.


If you're… Is it OK?


Adding or removing furniture Yes


Just say it's virtually staged


Showing new paint or floors Be clear


Say exactly what changed


Hiding cracks, stains, or damage No


That's hiding a problem


Adding a pool or view that isn't there No


Buyers will notice


Each Texas MLS has its own photo rules, so check yours before you upload. The safe habit everywhere: write "virtually staged" in the photo description and keep the originals.


3rd quarter


## The primary bedroom: show off the space


A big empty bedroom can actually look smaller in photos, because there's nothing in it to show the scale. Buyers start wondering if their king bed will even fit. The **Valley Bluff** bundle answers that with a big, comfy bed, a leather chair with its own footstool, and a red patterned rug that adds just a little bit of ranch.


Before


After


Selling a lake house? Try **Prairie** . The paddles on the wall do the talking.


4th quarter


## The back patio: where your listing wins


New builds come with fresh sod and one skinny tree tied to a stake. Your listing might have a live oak that's older than the builder, so show it off. The **Oakridge** bundle (under Exterior) adds lounge chairs, an outdoor sofa, and a coffee table. Buyers can practically smell the brisket.


Before


After


Final whistle, and the home team wins.


Overtime


## Buyers shopping from another state


Texas gets more state-to-state movers than anywhere except Florida, and many of them shop from their couch. For them, your photos are the tour. Stage every main room, show more than one angle (Apply Design keeps the furniture matching), and add a 360° tour if you can.


And to our new neighbors: welcome, y'all. No, you don't need cowboy boots. You'll probably buy some anyway.


The cost


## What it costs your seller


Rented furniture can cost thousands, and the bill keeps coming every month the house sits. Virtual staging is paid once, and nobody has to haul a sectional upstairs in August.


Rented furniture Apply Design


Cost $4,000 to $6,000 From $7 a photo


Ready in A few days About 15 minutes


Lasts 45 to 60 days, then more fees Yours to keep


New look New furniture, new bill Change it anytime


Rental prices are U.S. averages for an empty home. $7 is the DIY editor price when you buy 20+ coins; one-click Auto Staging is $10.50. Your first photo is free.


Postgame


## Questions agents ask us


Is virtual staging allowed in Texas?


Yes. As of November 2026, Texas has no special law about it. Your ads just can't mislead buyers, and you should follow your MLS's labeling rules.


Where do I say a photo is virtually staged?


Check your MLS, since each one has its own rules. Many agents put it in the photo description and the listing remarks.


Does staging really help a home sell?


Yes. In NAR's 2025 staging report, 83% of buyers' agents said staging helps buyers picture the home as their own, and almost half of sellers' agents said it helped homes sell faster.


How much does Apply Design cost?


From $7 a photo with the DIY editor, or $10.50 with one-click Auto Staging, when you buy 20 or more coins. Your first photo is free. That's less than a pound of brisket.


General information, not legal advice, as of November 2026. See[TREC's advertising rules](https://www.trec.texas.gov/article/trecs-advertising-rules-what-you-need-know) or ask your broker.
